title: Which Screen Dracula Are You, Actually?
dek: Eight actors, eight castles, eight completely different ways to ruin someone's night — pick your habits and we'll hand you your fangs.

quiz.intro: No wrong answers here — just answer like the monster you truly are.

questions.question: Someone new walks into the room. What's your actual first move?

answers.text: I stare. I don't blink. I don't need to say anything yet.
I circle them slowly like they're already mine.
I make direct, aching eye contact like I've waited centuries for this.
I introduce myself with old-world charm and a kiss on the hand.
My eyes go red and things get physical fast.
I weep about it across three centuries of unresolved grief.
I take it personally but stay devastatingly charming about it.
I retreat somewhere dark and get quietly, pitifully depressed.
Baroque gold everything, portraits of my dead wife everywhere.
Tasteful gothic elegance — think five-star haunted hotel.
A crumbling, freezing, rat-infested castle. On purpose.
A literal war fortress with a throne carved from swords.

questions.question: Your assistant/servant/sidekick messes up badly. What now?

answers.text: I forgive them smoothly — I need the help, and I'm gracious about it.
I barely register it. I'm too consumed by my own misery.
Loyalty is earned in battle. They better prove themselves.
I explode, guilt-trip them for centuries, then act like nothing happened.

questions.question: What's your idea of a perfect date?

answers.text: Honestly? I don't think I know how to do this anymore.
Defending a castle together against overwhelming odds.
Dramatic, chaotic, and somehow still about me the whole time.
Something ridiculous that ends in both of us laughing.

questions.question: Someone challenges your authority in front of others. Your move?

answers.text: I remind them, calmly, that I've conquered armies.
I go absolutely feral about it, immediately, no chill whatsoever.
I trip over a prop, everyone forgets what the argument even was.
I fix them with a stare until they forget what they said.

questions.question: Pick a soundtrack for your entrance.

answers.text: Something way too dramatic for the room, played way too loud.
A kazoo. I want a kazoo.
Total silence except for a single, unbearably slow line of dialogue.
Something orchestral, aggressive, and a little bit terrifying.

questions.question: How would your enemies describe you?

answers.text: A disaster. A lovable, incompetent disaster.
Quiet. Hypnotic. Somehow more terrifying for saying almost nothing.
A predator. Fast, physical, and genuinely frightening.
Tragic. Almost sympathetic, if he weren't also a monster.
My own theatrics. I love a slow reveal too much.
My temper. I go from zero to violent instantly.
I never got over my wife. Three hundred years later. Still not over it.
I fall in love too fast, too hard, every single time.

questions.question: Last one — what's your go-to look?

answers.text: Blood-red contacts and just enough menace to be scary.
Wild wigs, sunglasses, a whole different look every scene.
Dashing, romantic, borderline Byronic — Old Hollywood leading man.
Bald, rat-like, deeply unsettling — beauty was never the point.

results.name: Bela Lugosi
results.subtitle: Dracula (1931)
results.description: You don't need to raise your voice or move fast — you just stare, and people simply do what you say. Lugosi's slow, hypnotic, Hungarian-accented Count basically invented the template every vampire since has been ripping off, and you know exactly how much power there is in doing less.

results.name: Christopher Lee
results.subtitle: Dracula / Horror of Dracula (1958)
results.description: You're not subtle, and you don't want to be. Lee's Hammer-era Dracula traded Lugosi's hypnosis for red eyes, fangs, and pure physical menace, turning the Count into a genuinely dangerous predator rather than a polite houseguest — and honestly, that's you at a party too.

results.name: Gary Oldman
results.subtitle: Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992)
results.description: You're the one crying in the bathroom at the wedding, and everyone knows it. Oldman's Dracula reframed the character as a tragic romantic wrecked by centuries of grief, wild transformations and all, and you feel every bit of that operatic heartbreak.

results.name: Frank Langella
results.subtitle: Dracula (1979)
results.description: You walk into a room and it's basically over for everyone. Langella played the Count as a full gothic romantic leading man, seductive and genuinely swoon-worthy rather than purely frightening, and you carry that same devastating old-world charm.

results.name: Klaus Kinski
results.subtitle: Nosferatu the Vampyre (1979)
results.description: You're not scary so much as deeply, unshakably sad, and somehow that's worse. Kinski's rat-like, hollow-eyed Count is one of the only Draculas you almost feel bad for — mournful and pathetic instead of predatory — and that quiet misery is very on-brand for you.

results.name: Luke Evans
results.subtitle: Dracula Untold (2014)
results.description: You'd burn the world down to protect your people, and you have the battle scars to prove it. This version reimagined the Count as Vlad Tepes, a warrior-king who is not a black or white creature of the night, he's a family man and benevolent ruler who will stop at nothing in order to protect his kingdom — a good soldier before he was ever a monster, just like you.

results.name: Nicolas Cage
results.subtitle: Renfield (2023)
results.description: You're a lot. You know you're a lot. Cage's Dracula sips blood from a martini glass, guilt-trips his own familiar for centuries, and delivers a faux-aristocratic performance that sinks his acting teeth into the power of Dracula — unhinged, toxic, and never once boring, which is basically your whole personality.

results.name: Leslie Nielsen
results.subtitle: Dracula: Dead and Loving It (1995)
results.description: You cannot take anything seriously, including your own doom, and that's exactly why people love you. Nielsen's full spoof-Dracula turned the gothic icon into pure slapstick, and you'd rather trip over your own cape than ever be genuinely scary.
